text: Problem set 9 Problem 1. Are the following matrices diagonalizable over R? Over C? If yes, find the invertible matrix P ∈ Mn×n(R) or Mn×n(C) such that P −1AP = diag(λ1, . . . , λn). If no, give the reason.( 5 −3 6 −4 ) , ( 2 2 −1 0 ) , ( 0 1 −4 4 ) . Problem 2. Suppose T : R3 → R3 is linear and −4, 5, and √7 are all eigenvalues of T . Prove that there exists x ∈ R3 such that T x − 9x = (−4, 5, √7)t. Hint: The right hand side (−4, 5, √7)t is a distraction. In fact you would only need to show that T − 9I is invertible. Problem 3. (i) If z, w ∈ C show that Re z = 1 2 (z + ¯z), Im z = 1 2i (z − ¯z), z + w = z + w and zw = ¯z ¯w. (ii) If A, C ∈ Mm×n(C) and B ∈ Mn×p(C), show that Re A = 1 2 (A + ¯A), Im A = 1 2i (A − ¯A), A + C = ¯A + ¯C and AB = ¯A ¯B. (iii) If A ∈ Mn×n(C), show that det( ¯A) = det(A). Problem 4. Let λ0, . . . , λn be distinct points in R. Let p0, . . . , pn be the polynomials in Pn(R) defined uniquely by the relations pi(λj) = δij, ∀i, j ∈ {0, . . . , n}, (1) where δij is the Kronecker delta. (i) Show that pi(x) = (x − λ0) · · · (x − λi−1)(x − λi+1) · · · (x − λn) (λi − λ0) · · · (λi − λi−1)(λi − λi+1) · · · (λi − λn) . Hint: Observe that λ0, . . . , λi−1, λi+1, . . . , λn are roots of pi and use Proposition 9.10 and degree to show that pi(x) = c(x − λ0) · · · (x − λi−1)(x − λi+1) · · · (x − λn) for some c ∈ R. Determine the value of c using pi(λi) = 1. (ii) Show that p0, . . . , pn are linearly independent in Pn(R). Hint: It’s easier to evaluate the linear combination of p0, . . . , pn at λi using (1) than trying to find the coordinates of pi under the standard basis. (iii) We define φi : Pn(R) → R given by φi(f ) = f (λi). From Homework 5 Problem 4, we know that φi is a linear function i.e. φi ∈ V ∗. Conclude that φ0, . . . , φn is the dual basis of p0, . . . , pn. (iv) Show that for any p(x) ∈ Pn(R), p(x) = ∑n i=0 p(λi)pi. This is the Lagrange interpolation formula. (v) Show that the change of basis matrix from p0, . . . , pn to the standard basis of Pn(R) is        1 λ0 λ2 0 · · · λ n 0 1 λ1 λ2 1 · · · λ n 1 1 λ2 λ2 2 · · · λ n 2 ... ... ... . . . ... 1 λn λ2 n · · · λ n n        . 1 This is called the Vandermonde matrix. Optional exercises related to Lecture 9 Do NOT submit this with your homework. The following problems are from Linear algebra done right. 1. Exercise 1B: 8, Exercise 3B: 33 Exercise 5A: 17, 18 Remark 1. Exercise 1B: 8 and 3B: 33 answer the question: we can view A ∈ Mn×n(R) as a matrix A ∈ Mn×n(C) easily but what is the vector space over C that the linear transformation acting on? In other words, if T : V → V is a linear transformation on a vector space V over R, how do we view T as a linear transfor- mation on some vector space over C where T has the same matrix representation under a basis? Exercises 5A: 17,18 are simply restatements of the results we proved in class using matrices, now expressed in the language of linear transformations. 2. Exercise 4: 8,11,14. Remark 2. Exercise 4: 8 is a very useful test whether a polynomial has repeated roots. Exercise 4: 14 is an interesting proof of the Bezout identity. 3. Exercise 5A: 9, 19, 20 Remark 3. In infinite dimensional space, characteristic polynomials are not avail- able. One can only use the definition to find eigenvalues and eigenvectors. There could be infinitely many eigenvalues or no eigenvalues at all regardless of the choice of the field. 2
